newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FORECAST - Newcrest H1 results to halve.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FORECAST - Newcrest H1 results to halve.

text.p: Lower output and higher costs are expected to almost halve Newcrest Mining Ltd's half-year profit amid speculation the embattled gold miner may become a takeover target, share analysts said Tuesday.
Newcrest's pre-abnormal net profit for the six months to December 31 was forecast at an average of A$6.4 million, compared with A$12 million a year earlier.
Analysts' forecasts ranged from A$4.7 million to A$8.0 million.

Newcrest, which chalked up unaudited net profits of A$9.6 million in its first financial quarter, warned last month it would post an audited loss before tax and abnormals of A$4.8 million for the second quarter.
Analysts blamed the earnings slide on a 12.5 percent drop in gold output to 263,359 ounces for the half, coupled with a rise in operating costs to A$500 an ounce from A$494 previously.

They said Newcrest's main gold operation, Telfer in Western Australia, performed particularly poorly with continued problems at its number five leach pad and lower feed grades dashing hopes of improved output there in 1996/97 (July/June).
Persistent heavy rains have added to the mine's woes in the current half, forcing Newcrest to scale back and then suspend operations for two weeks from Monday.
"Telfer went awfully and Telfer's going to kill them again this half," said Bell Securities gold analyst Keith Goode.
Analysts said abnormal items would do little to mask Newcrest's tepid operating performance.

The company expects to book an after-tax abnormal gain of A$144.4 million from gold hedging but this is expected to be largely offset by a planned writedown of its 12 percent stake in fellow gold miner Normandy Mining Ltd.
Normandy's Tuesday closing price of A$1.78 values Newcrest's holding at A$344.1 million, giving it a paper loss of A$105.9 million on the investment it made in March last year.
But few analysts' agreed on the size of the writedown with pre-tax expectations ranging from A$100 million to A$150 million.
"The abnormals are going to throw (the bottom line) all over the place," Goode said.
Newcrest's underperformance and uncertain outlook has left its shares about 26 percent below last year's high of A$6.62 and struggling to recover.
The weak price has led some analysts to speculate the company might be vulnerable to a hostile takeover, possibly from North American gold companies.
"They are all out there hungry for reserve ounces. Newcrest has a lot of them and relatively cheaply as well," said one Melbourne-based gold analyst who declined to be named.
A Sydney analyst said it would not be beyond Newcrest's former major shareholder, U.S.-based Newmont Mining Corp, to make a play for the company it sold out of in early 1993.
However, some analysts said a bid was unlikely, citing issues such as the Normandy stake and problematic Telfer mine as reasons for a predator to look elsewhere.
Newcrest is expected to announce its half-year results on Thursday.
-- Melbourne bureau 61-3 9286-1435
